name: No AI Only Grades
title: No AI Only Grades
answer: No AI Only Grades means that every grade a student receives must be a decision made and confirmed by a teacher, never assigned by an AI tool on its own. AI can speed up grading and offer a second opinion, but the teacher scores the work first and stays the final judge. This matters because grades shape course placement and college admission, so an unconfirmed machine score could affect a student's future.

sections.body: This idea sets a firm rule for grading: AI may help teachers work faster, but it must never issue a grade that the teacher has not personally confirmed. The problem is that AI scoring does not read student work the way teachers do, and automated essay scoring tools have been found to weigh features of writing differently from the priorities set out in human rubrics. If a school lets a tool's score stand as the grade, that score may not mean what it claims to mean. The rule keeps the professional judgment of the teacher at the center of every grade that goes on a student's record.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day classroom use, the teacher scores the work first and then turns to AI only as a check on that judgment, not as the source of the grade. Lower risk uses fit easily into this pattern: a teacher can collect short answers through Google Forms, have AI sort the responses into groups of similar answers, and then read and score every answer, which is still the teacher's work but faster. After a test, item analysis can reveal which questions many students missed, which helps the teacher plan reteaching. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the same order of decisions applies across year levels: teacher decides, machine checks.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support. A study of automated essay scoring with language models found that the tools weighted features of writing differently from the priorities in human rubrics, raising concerns about whether the scores meant what they claimed (Wang et al., 2026). Researchers have also proposed frameworks to test the reliability and alignment of these tools (Liu et al., 2026). On the order of decisions, research has shown that when a machine decides first and a person is meant to check, people rarely correct the machine's errors (Krugel et al., 2023), while when the person decides first and the machine offers a second opinion, people keep their own judgment. Until a tool has been tested against a school's own rubrics, its scores are suggestions at best.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are firm. AI should never assign a grade the teacher has not confirmed, and until a tool has been tested against the school's own rubrics its scores are only suggestions. The risk of reversing the order is real: when the machine decides first, people tend not to correct its errors, so the teacher's judgment quietly disappears. The decisions that stay with a person are the scoring of the work and the final grade, with AI kept to a checking role and to lower risk tasks such as grouping similar responses or surfacing patterns in test results.
